relevant_pages.reason: Describes harms from misleading or hard‑to‑understand information and introduces the Consumer Duty aimed at enabling informed consumer decisions
Sets out overarching Consumer Principle and cross‑cutting rules including acting in good faith and avoiding foreseeable harm, which communications can breach
Defines high‑level outcomes including fair value, suitability and treatment, confidence and access that apply to how firms inform and treat consumers
States that consumers must be equipped with the right information to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions about products and services
Mentions risk that unclear outcomes‑based regulation could lead firms to withdraw products, implying expectations on fair access and communications about availability
Mentions that firms can change communications to reflect different standards for in-scope and out-of-scope customers, implying expectations about tailoring communications
Discusses developing different communications for retail and non‑retail customer groups, indicating expectations on tailoring and segmentation of communications content
Defines when firms are responsible for preparing and approving communications to retail customers as a material influence on customer outcomes
States that incorrectly classifying a product as non‑retail to avoid the Duty and then distributing it to retail customers would breach the Duty, which can be assessed via how the product is marketed
Clarifies that the Duty applies to ancillary activities such as product design and ongoing customer support, both of which can include communications whose content and fairness are auditable

Explains identified harms in e‑money and payment services including problems with firm communications and clarifies that only communications aspects of the Duty apply to certain mortgages, setting checkable expectations for communications content and standards
discusses application of the consumer understanding and consumer support outcome rules to existing and closed products, which govern standards for communications and support content
introduces the new Consumer Principle requiring firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, an overarching conduct standard that marketing and communications content could breach
explains the meaning of ‘good outcomes’ under the Consumer Principle, setting an objective conduct standard that marketing communications must align with
clarifies that consumers must have the information and support they need to make informed decisions, implying expectations on clarity and sufficiency of communications

describes how the Duty is outcomes‑based and proportionate, with firms expected to act in good faith and deliver good outcomes, which can be assessed against the content and tone of consumer‑facing communications
links existing TCF guidance and Principle 7 (communications) to the higher Consumer Duty standard, affecting expectations on fairness and clarity of communications
defines the good faith cross‑cutting rule as honesty, fair and open dealing and consistency with reasonable customer expectations, which can be assessed in marketing text
states that customers’ reasonable expectations depend on product nature and firm’s prior communications, and references cross‑cutting rules and culture relevant to how communications are framed
explains firms must consider consumers’ limited experience and behavioural biases and that consumer understanding rules require monitoring communications so customers understand them

requires firms to establish an environment where consumers can act in their own interests, taking account of behavioural biases and vulnerability characteristics, which constrains how communications are designed

discusses considering needs and characteristics (eg visual impairment, bereavement, low financial capability) and suggests inclusive design, which has implications for accessibility and framing of communications

addresses the limits of using additional disclosure to mitigate harm and warns about information overload and complexity, providing principles for how disclosures and communications should be structured

states that consumer‑visible product features must be understandable by the target market and discusses using amended communications, testing understanding, and monitoring outcomes to address harms, all directly governing communication content and clarity

sets a fairness principle on price and value that marketing claims about value or benefits must not conflict with, enabling audits of whether promotional messaging fairly reflects the relationship between price and benefit
states overarching expectations that communications give consumers needed information at the right time and in a way they can understand
sets content and presentation expectations for communications, including layered approaches and clarity so explanations are likely to be understood
discusses how firms can support consumer understanding within advice/marketing and data‑protection constraints, including what information may be sent
requires communications to be understandable by the intended recipients and to account for vulnerability characteristics when drafting and presenting information
imposes obligations to tailor one‑to‑one communications and explains expectations for testing whether communications enable understanding of key features, costs and risks
clarifies testing obligations for communications, including when firms should test and that they must ensure communications support understanding even where mandatory disclosures apply
sets expectations that communications clearly disclose limited support channels and that firms adapt communication formats to meet vulnerable customers’ needs
states that unclear or confusing digital customer journeys will not meet standards and requires clear communication of support limitations and reasonable adjustments for disabled consumers
introduces guidance that when declining access to a product, firms should provide information or signposting to help customers meet financial objectives, affecting declinature communications
notes that large volumes of marketing and customer communications must be reviewed and potentially amended for Duty compliance, highlighting scope though not detailed content rules
mentions reviewing the most significant communications first when prioritising implementation work
states firms should prioritise reviewing the most significant communications, implying expectations about communication content that may breach the Duty
mentions consumers being put in a position to make informed decisions, implying expectations about information provided in firm communications and disclosures
Defines ‘non-retail financial instrument’ partly by required marketing-material disclosures about eligible investors and retail-intent, which are checkable in communications

Continues definition of ‘non-retail financial instrument’ including obligations about how promotional communications are directed, and defines ‘product’ in a way that scopes which communications rules apply
Defines ‘retail market business’ and excludes certain offers and associated promotional communications, scoping when communication rules apply
Glossary definition of ‘financial promotion rules’ points to Principles 7 and 12 and PRIN 2A communication requirements, directly scoping which communications are subject to content rules
sets out Principles 7 and 12 on communications and consumer duty, including ‘clear, fair and not misleading’ standard relevant to marketing materials
describes Consumer Duty scope and interpretive standards that govern how communications and consumer outcomes should be assessed
defines ‘acting in good faith’ including not manipulating or exploiting customers via how information is presented, directly constraining marketing content
explains foreseeable harm including requirements around product marketing and information provided to customers
cross‑cutting obligation to enable and support customers includes how information and product marketing are designed and provided throughout the customer journey
states that cross‑cutting obligations apply at all stages of the customer journey, implicating all customer-facing communications
states that cross‑cutting obligations apply when designing communications to the target market, defining expectations that can be breached by the content or design of communications
defines ‘value’ and fair value in relation to what customers pay and the benefits reasonably expected, which can constrain promotional claims about price and value in marketing materials

links value assessments to when a product is marketed or distributed and defines expected total price components, affecting how price, fees and non‑financial costs should be represented in communications
clarifies that non‑financial costs include provision and use of personal data, which can drive required transparency around data‑use communicated in marketing or customer information

requires manufacturers to give distributors necessary information to understand intended value and requires distributors’ arrangements to align with fair value, constraining how benefits, price and value are described in customer‑facing materials

Sets broad obligations on all retail customer communications to be clear, fair, not misleading, meet information needs, be timely and understandable, which can be audited directly against marketing text

Contains detailed principles on how information must be presented (plain language, prominence, avoiding unnecessary disclaimers, appropriate detail) that can be checked against the content and layout of marketing and consumer communications

Requires tailoring of communications to customer characteristics and one-to-one interactions, and mandates certain questions/checks during dialogues, all assessable from scripts and communication content
Imposes obligations to test, monitor, and adapt communications where they are not supporting good outcomes, partially checkable via reviewing specific communications and how they were changed

Requires firms to notify issues with other firms’ communications and to provide information so it can be communicated to retail customers, which touches on the content passed through the chain for customer-facing communications

Customer support duties include providing sufficient opportunity to understand and assess options, and avoiding unreasonable barriers in journeys such as cancellation; some of this can be assessed from wording and structure of support communications and scripts

Examples of unreasonable barriers and delays (e.g. disproportionately longer call times to cancel than buy) and duty to support representatives; parts can be audited from customer communication scripts and messaging tone/content

sets general standard for prudent firms including duties to promote, monitor and support consumer understanding in light of product risk and complexity, which governs content and presentation of communications

defines monitoring obligations specifically for communications and whether customers have the right information to make effective, timely and informed decisions, reflecting expectations on marketing/communication content
requires firms to explain harm and remedial actions to customers in a way that is fair, clear and not misleading, setting a checkable communication standard for such notices
links Principle 12 and PRIN 2A, including communication and financial promotions, to MiFID business and specifies their application to communication/approval of financial promotions
references application of Principles including 6, 7 and 12 in relation to communication and approval of financial promotions, which govern content and standards of communications
addresses interaction and scope of Principles 6, 7 and 12, which include fair, clear and not misleading communication standards relevant to marketing content
clarifies that guarantors are treated as retail customers for Principles 6, 7 and 12, affecting how marketing and customer communications must address them
discusses disapplication/limitation of Principles including 6, 7 and 12 for MiFID business, which affects when marketing-communication content rules apply
introduces COCON Rule 6 duty to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, an overarching conduct principle that marketing texts themselves could breach
further scopes where Rule 6 (good outcomes for retail customers) applies and its interaction with Rule 4 (treat customers fairly), setting principles relevant to communications
states that where Rule 6 applies, Rule 4 (treat customers fairly) does not, shaping which overarching conduct standard governs communications

defines obligations under Individual Conduct Rule 6 including good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, and supporting customers’ financial objectives, principles that marketing communications can breach
links Rule 6 interpretation to PRIN 2A cross-cutting obligations and outcomes rules, including foreseeable harm examples relevant to how communications in a distribution chain may cause harm
Rule 6 guidance about delivering good outcomes for retail customers, which can be breached by misleading or unfair communications
explains how staff conduct and responsibilities relate to outcomes experienced by retail customers, including through scripted interactions and communications
highlights influence of salespersons and customer support staff on customer outcomes, which includes their communications with customers
links PROD to Principle 12 and PRIN 2A, which contain rules on fair, clear, non‑misleading and outcome-focused customer communications
